why.text_en: The main birthday wish. Word for word "all the best for the birthday". You say it as a whole; there's no verb in it.
why.why_de_en: A wish with no verb: Alles Gute — all the best, zum Geburtstag — for the birthday. Germans say it as a whole.
why.why_en: English: Happy birthday! German: Alles Gute zum Geburtstag! — word for word "All the best for the birthday". Learn it as one block.

why_not.en: Don't translate "happy" word for word: "Glücklicher Geburtstag" isn't said. The wish is "all the best for" the day: zum Geburtstag.

why.why_voice_en: The main birthday wish. Word for word "all the best for the birthday". You say it as a whole; there's no verb in it.

why.text_en: The second wish: "heartfelt good-luck wish". Glückwunsch is a der-word, so Herzlichen ends in -en, like Guten Tag.
why.why_de_en: A wish with no verb, said as a whole. Glückwunsch is a der-word, so Herzlichen, not Herzliche.
why.why_en: English: Congratulations! — one word. German: Herzlichen Glückwunsch! — "heartfelt luck-wish". English "good" never changes; German Herzlich- gets -en.

why_not.en: A common mistake is Herzliche instead of Herzlichen. Glückwunsch is a der-word: in a wish it takes Herzlichen.

why.why_voice_en: The second wish: "heartfelt good-luck wish". Glückwunsch is a der-word, so Herzlichen ends in -en, like Guten Tag.

why.text_en: You "have" your birthday: ich habe Geburtstag. heute — "today" — comes right after the verb.
why.why_de_en: ich · habe · heute · Geburtstag: the verb habe is car 2. You "have" your birthday: ich habe Geburtstag.
why.why_en: English: It's my birthday today. German: "I have today birthday" — Ich habe heute Geburtstag. No "it's", no "my".

why_not.en: The mistake is bin: "Ich bin Geburtstag" means you yourself are the birthday. You say ich habe Geburtstag.

why.why_voice_en: You "have" your birthday: ich habe Geburtstag. heute — "today" — comes right after the verb.

why.text_en: für dich — "for you". You say this when handing over a present: das ist für dich.
why.why_de_en: Das · ist · für dich: the verb ist is car 2, the anchor of the whole sentence.
why.why_en: Exactly like English: Das ist für dich — This is for you. After für, "you" is dich (du → dich).

why_not.en: Don't drop ist: "Das für dich" is a fragment, just like "This for you" in English.

why.root_en: ist and English "is" share one ancient root *es- (DWDS, Wiktionary)
why.why_voice_en: für dich — "for you". You say this when handing over a present: das ist für dich.

why.text_en: das Geschenk is a das-word, so ein Geschenk: one present. ist works like an "=" sign.
why.why_de_en: ist works like an "=" sign: das = ein Geschenk. The verb holds car 2. The right side has the same role as "who", so the article doesn't change: ein Geschenk.
why.why_en: Just like English: Das ist ein Geschenk — This is a present. Careful: Gift in German means "poison", a present is Geschenk!

why_not.en: Don't drop ist: "Das ein Geschenk" is a fragment, just like "This a present" in English.

why.root_en: ist and English "is" share one ancient root *es- (DWDS, Wiktionary)
why.why_voice_en: das Geschenk is a das-word, so ein Geschenk: one present. ist works like an "=" sign.

why.text_en: Glück means both "happiness" and "luck". People say Viel Glück on a birthday, before an exam and before a trip.
why.why_de_en: A wish with no verb: Viel Glück — much happiness, luck. Glück isn't counted, so there's no article.
why.why_en: English: Good luck! German: Viel Glück! — word for word "much luck". Glück sounds like English "luck" with a G in front.

why_not.en: The mistake is Viele. Viele is for things you count. Glück isn't counted, so Viel — like "much" vs "many".

why.why_voice_en: Glück means both "happiness" and "luck". People say Viel Glück on a birthday, before an exam and before a trip.

why.text_en: A wish for a "good night". die Nacht is a die-word, so Gute.

why.why_en: English "good" never changes: good day, good night. German does: Guten Tag (der Tag), but Gute Nacht — Good night (die Nacht).

why_not.en: A common mistake: carrying Guten over from the morning to the night. Nacht is a die-word, so Gute.

why_not.en: Not a mistake, but it sounds different: that's how you ask back in surprise ("You have WhatsApp?!"). A normal question puts the verb first.

why.why_de_en: The question word Woher takes car 1, the verb kommst comes right after it in car 2: Woher kommst du? A German says first WHAT he wants to know.
why.why_en: English: Where are you from? — with "are". German uses "come": Woher kommst du? — word for word "Where-from come you?"

why_not.en: du got in front of kommst — the verb left car 2. After Woher a German expects the verb at once, otherwise it is not a question.

why.why_de_en: Ich · lerne · Deutsch: the verb lerne is car 2, the anchor of the whole sentence.
why.why_en: Same order as English: Ich lerne Deutsch — I'm learning German. German has no "am …-ing": lerne means both "learn" and "am learning".

why_not.en: The verb lerne went to the end. That's how the tail of a long sentence sounds after "dass" (that) or "weil" (because); in a simple sentence lerne is car 2.

ch11_L1_why_1.answer_en: You "have" your birthday: ich habe Geburtstag.
distractors_en: habe always goes before the word heute.

ch11_L1_why_2.answer_en: Glückwunsch is a der-word, and in a wish it takes -en before it.
distractors_en: Glückwunsch is a die-word, and in a wish it takes -en before it.
-en is added to all words with a capital letter.

ch11_L1_why_3.prompt_en: Why is there no article in "Viel Glück"?
distractors_en: Only the word Geschenk needs an article.

ch11_L1_why_4.answer_en: Geschenk is a das-word, so ein.
distractors_en: Geschenk is a die-word, and eine is rarely written.

ch11_L1_why_5.prompt_en: Why does "Das ist für dich" need "ist"?
ch11_L1_why_5.answer_en: No verb, no sentence: ist holds car 2.
distractors_en: ist means "for" here, so it goes at the start.
ist goes after für and before dich.

ch11_L1_boss_1.prompt_en: Why does the verb in "Ja, ich habe heute Geburtstag" come after ich and not after Ja?
ch11_L1_boss_1.answer_en: Ja takes no car: ich is car 1, habe is car 2.
distractors_en: Ja is the first word, and the verb is always third.
The word heute must come before habe.

Goal: congratulate her and give her a present.
data.voice_en: In Germany people congratulate you in person on your birthday: at work and at the course you bring coffee and cake. Today it's Olga's birthday. You'll congratulate her and give her a present.
data.hook_en: Lesson riddle: in English you say "It's my birthday". Why does a German say Ich habe Geburtstag — "I have birthday"?
data.anime_motif_en: isekai: the first holiday in a new world — the hero gives a present for the first time and says the words out loud (no quotes)
data.more_en: Sofia will ask Olga about her birthday. You'll congratulate Olga and say "This is for you". The teacher will wish her luck.
data.goal_en: After this lesson you can: wish someone a happy birthday, say "it's my birthday today" and hand over a gift with "This is for you".

data.trap_en: Glück means both "happiness" and "luck". People say Viel Glück on a birthday, before an exam and before a trip.

data.life_detail_en: Germans don't congratulate in advance: by custom, wishing someone well before the actual birthday brings bad luck. At work the birthday person treats everyone — usually to coffee and cake (Goethe-Institut, "Texte Geburtstag", goethe.de/resources/files/pdf81/Texte_Geburtstag.pdf).

data.book_note_en: The rule goes into the "Spell Book" once it becomes "solid" (after reviews).
data.voice_en: English says "it's my birthday". A German says ich habe Geburtstag, word for word "I have birthday" — with no article. Like WhatsApp: ich habe.
screen_en: Ich · habe · heute · Geburtstag. — "I have birthday today"
Ich · habe · WhatsApp. — the same train
data.answer_hook_en: Answer to the riddle: you "have" your birthday. Ich habe WhatsApp — Ich habe heute Geburtstag: the verb habe is in car 2.

second.voice_en: Glückwunsch takes der. In a wish, Herzlichen goes before it, with the ending -en. A die-word would take a different form.

data.prompt_en: Build it yourself from pieces you know: you're giving Olga a present. Say: "This is a present for you." The verb ist is car 2.

data.tip_en: The letter ü is neither "oo" nor "ee". Say "ee" without moving your tongue, and round your lips as for "oo". That's ü: für, Glück.
data.bridge_en: English has no such sound: "oo" pulls the tongue back, "ee" pushes it forward. German ü has the tongue of "ee" and the lips of "oo" — like French "tu".

data.note_en: Congratulate Olga with either wish — the AI accepts both: Alles Gute zum Geburtstag! or Herzlichen Glückwunsch!
data.rule_en: the AI only uses sentences shown in parts 3–4 (WORLD §4.1)

data.task_en: A newcomer heard Sofia say "Olga, hast du heute Geburtstag?" and is looking up hast in a dictionary. Explain to him in English what she asked.
data.expected_en: Olga, is it your birthday today?
data.hint_en: Geburtstag — birthday; hast du — "do you have"; heute — today; together — "is it your birthday today?"
data.ai_checks_en: is it clear and is the meaning right (not word for word)
data.level_note_en: A1.1 — we explain in English; later — in German

data.tip_en: Geburtstag, Geschenk, Glück, Glückwunsch are things — capital letter. Glück and für have ü with two dots, not u. For the ü sound always write ü.

screen_en: The party table is up: you congratulated Olga and gave her a present.
Tip for tomorrow: wish someone a happy birthday out loud — Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!

data.next_hook_en: Next: Olga will ask "Wem gratulierst du?" — and the word dem will appear before Chef. Where it comes from — in the next lesson.
